chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Life of an ESOP

lessons.title: Resignation, Termination and Acquisition: What Happens to Your ESOPs

children.text: Every ESOP conversation is optimistic until someone leaves. Resignation, a layoff, a takeover: each one rewrites what you hold, usually within days, and almost always on terms that were fixed long before, in a document you signed without reading.
This lesson covers the four exits that actually happen: you quit, you are let go, something happens to you, or somebody buys the company.

body.text: The day you stop being an employee, unvested options are gone and vested options start a countdown. Everything now depends on two lines in your scheme: how you left, and how long your exercise window runs.

children.text: The Leaver Matrix

Indian law sets the outer limits, and your scheme fills in the rest. Under the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, options that have not vested expire when you resign or your employment is terminated, while vested options remain exercisable for the period the scheme and the board specify. Death and permanent incapacity are treated very differently, and much more kindly.

body.caption: What happens to your options, by type of exit

cells: Retained, must be exercised in the window
Lapse, though some companies accelerate as a gesture
Often cancelled as well, if the scheme says so
Depends entirely on the scheme and board discretion
Usually retained, sometimes with a longer window
Pass to the legal heirs or nominee
All options vest on that date

body.text: The death and permanent incapacity provisions are protective by law, not by company kindness. If you hold a meaningful ESOP, make sure your nomination details with the company are filled in and current. A missing nomination turns a clean entitlement into a succession dispute.

children.text: Resignation: The Window Is the Whole Story
Vested options survive your resignation. What kills them is the
exercise window
: the short period, often 30 to 90 days from your last working day, in which you must pay up or lose them.

markDefs.definition: The limited period after your last working day in which you may still exercise vested options. Miss it and they lapse.

children.text: Consider the arithmetic that lands on a leaver with 8,000 vested options at ₹15 when the fair market value is ₹190.

stats.label: Total cash needed
stats.context: Within 30 days, while also changing jobs

body.text: A short exercise window at an unlisted company is a quiet way of taking back what you earned. You must fund the exercise price and the tax within weeks, for shares you cannot sell. Many employees simply let the options lapse. Ask about the window before you join, not on your last day.

body.title: What to Ask HR the Week You Resign
steps: Exactly how many options are vested as of my last working day?
When does my exercise window open and close, in dates?
Can the window be extended, and who approves that?
What is the current fair market value, and when does that valuation expire?
Can I exercise partially, and is there a minimum lot?
How will the perquisite tax be collected once I am off payroll?
Will I be included in any upcoming buyback or secondary sale?

children.text: Termination: Good Leaver, Bad Leaver
Most schemes divide the world into a
good leaver
and a
bad leaver
. A good leaver keeps vested options and exercises them in the window. A bad leaver can lose everything, including options already vested, and can face a
clawback
of shares already issued, often repurchased at face value.

markDefs.definition: An employee who leaves on ordinary terms, such as resignation or retirement, and keeps their vested options subject to the exercise window.
An employee who leaves in circumstances defined in the scheme, such as termination for misconduct or breach, and can lose even vested options.
A scheme provision allowing the company to cancel options or repurchase shares, often at a nominal price, in defined circumstances.

body.title: What counts as a bad leaver, and why it matters more than it looks

children.text: Typical triggers are termination for misconduct or fraud, breach of the employment agreement, breach of confidentiality, and sometimes joining a named competitor within a defined period. The definitions are written by the company and can be broad.

The point to grasp is that a bad leaver clause can reach vested options and even shares you have already paid for. Two questions are worth asking before you sign: how exactly is cause defined, and who decides whether it applies. If the answer is that the board decides in its sole discretion, you are holding a weaker instrument than the grant letter suggests.

Non-compete restrictions in India are generally hard to enforce against an employee after employment ends, but an ESOP scheme does not need a court to act. It can simply cancel the options under its own terms.

body.title: Which Clause Bites?
body.question: Sandeep is asked to leave in a cost-cutting exercise. He has 2,000 vested and 6,000 unvested options. His scheme has a standard leaver clause with no misconduct allegation. What is the most likely outcome?
options: Both vested and unvested options are cancelled because he did not resign voluntarily
All 8,000 options vest immediately because the company initiated the exit
The 6,000 unvested options lapse, and he may exercise the 2,000 vested ones within his window
He keeps everything until the original expiry date
body.explanation: Unvested options lapse on cessation of employment, and vested options survive but must be exercised within the scheme window. Some companies do voluntarily accelerate vesting in a layoff, and it is always worth asking, but nothing in the rules requires it.

children.text: Acquisition: Four Possible Endings
When a buyer arrives, your options can go in four directions. The scheme, the share purchase agreement and the buyer’s appetite decide which.
Cash out.
The buyer pays you the deal price minus your exercise price for vested options. Clean and immediate.
Assumption or exchange.
Your options are replaced with options over the acquirer’s shares, with vesting carried over. Common when a listed company buys a startup.
Acceleration.
Vesting speeds up, fully or partly, so more of your grant becomes real before the deal closes.
Cancellation.
Unvested options, and occasionally out-of-the-money vested ones, are simply cancelled.

body.title: Single trigger vs double trigger acceleration

columns.label: Single trigger
points: Vesting accelerates on the acquisition alone
Buyers dislike it, since the team is paid before the work is done
Rare in Indian grants outside founder-level terms

columns.label: Double trigger
points: Needs the acquisition plus your exit or demotion soon after
Protects you if the buyer restructures you out
Keeps you incentivised to stay through integration
The fairest structure, and the one worth negotiating for

children.text: What an acquisition payout looks like
Suppose a buyer values the company at ₹450 a share and you hold 5,000 vested options at an exercise price of ₹40.

body.caption: (₹450 minus ₹40) × 5,000 = ₹20,50,000, before tax. The tax follows the same perquisite and capital gains logic covered in Chapter 4.

body.title: Value the Cash-Out
body.prompt: An acquirer offers ₹450 per share. You hold 5,000 vested options with an exercise price of ₹40, and the deal cashes out vested options. What is your pre-tax payout?
body.explanation: ₹410 of value per option × 5,000 options = ₹20,50,000. Your unvested options are a separate question, and depend on whether the deal accelerates them, assumes them or cancels them.

children.text: The Deal Indian Employees Still Talk About

When Walmart bought Flipkart in 2018, the transaction included a large purchase of employee stock options rather than leaving staff to wait for a distant listing. It became the reference point for what a good acquisition outcome looks like in India.

body.title: How the Flipkart payout was staged

events.title: Deal announced
events.description: Walmart agreed to acquire a controlling stake in Flipkart, and a buyback of vested employee options was announced to staff.

events.title: First liquidation
events.description: Current employees could liquidate 50% of their vested options.

events.title: Second window
events.description: A further 25% of vested options could be liquidated.

events.title: Final window
events.description: The remaining 25% became available, keeping employees invested through the integration.

children.text: Notice the staging. Even in a generous outcome, the buyer spread payments over two years to retain people. An acquisition is rarely a single payday, and employees who left early typically received only the first slice.

body.title: The Offer Arrives Mid-Acquisition
body.scenario: Aarti is a senior engineer at a Chennai SaaS company being acquired by a listed US firm. She has 9,000 vested and 15,000 unvested options at a ₹30 exercise price, and the deal values shares at ₹380. Her scheme has double trigger acceleration. A competitor offers her a role with a ₹12 lakh higher salary, starting next month. The acquisition closes in about four months.
body.prompt: What should she weigh before answering the competitor?
body.modelAnswer: Her vested options are worth roughly 9,000 × ₹350 = ₹31,50,000 before tax, and leaving now starts her exercise window immediately, so she would have to fund the exercise price and perquisite tax within weeks while the shares are still unlisted. Her 15,000 unvested options are worth about ₹52,50,000 of pre-tax value at the deal price, and her double trigger protects them only if she is still employed when the deal closes and is then let go or demoted. Resigning before closing forfeits all of it. The four-month gap is the crux: a ₹12 lakh salary increase is worth ₹4 lakh over four months, against a much larger sum at stake in unvested value. The sensible move is to ask the competitor to defer the start date, and separately to ask her employer in writing what the deal does to unvested options and whether retention terms are being offered. If the competitor cannot wait and the acquirer offers nothing in writing, she is choosing between a certain salary gain and an uncertain but far larger equity outcome.

points: Unvested options lapse when you resign or are terminated. Vested options survive, but only for the length of your exercise window.
A 30 to 90 day window at an unlisted company can force a large cash and tax outflow for shares you cannot sell.
Death and permanent incapacity while in employment trigger immediate vesting under Indian rules, with death entitlements passing to legal heirs or nominees, so keep your nomination current.
Bad leaver clauses can cancel even vested options and claw back shares. Check how cause is defined and who decides.
An acquisition can cash out, assume, accelerate or cancel your options, and the scheme decides which.
Double trigger acceleration, needing both the deal and your exit, is the structure worth negotiating for.
Even the Flipkart payout was staged over two years, so treat an acquisition as a process, not a single payday.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Leaver terms, windows and acquisition treatment vary by scheme and by deal. Figures are illustrative and the tax rate used is a simplified 31.2%. Read your scheme document and take professional advice before acting.
